interaction_type.value: dissociation of perfect dislocations into Shockley partial dislocations separated by a stacking fault

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: Multiple paired measurements of partial dislocation separation d and perfect dislocation character angle α were recorded along several dislocations in the base alloy; the paired (d, α) data were input into Eq. (1) to calculate SFE. Partial dislocation separation increases with dislocation angle. Figure 1 shows an example WBDF image with d and α marked and g//b condition (scale bar 50 nm).

slip_behavior.value: Dissociated dislocations in {111} planes; grains near a {111} orientation, which had favourable slip conditions during compression, were selected. WBDF imaging used g3g conditions with (220)-type reflections (s_g ≈ 0.22 nm^-1). Dissociated dislocations were confirmed to lie in the {111} plane approximately normal to the electron beam via g·b_p analysis.

interface_notes.value: The steel is single-phase austenite, so there are no interphase interfaces; the relevant planar 'interfaces' are stacking faults between the partial dislocations whose separation determines the SFE. Measured partial separations were not corrected for 2-D image projection because dissociated dislocations in this configuration are minimally inclined to the electron beam.

Material lattice parameter from discarding the lowest and highest a0 and averaging the remaining five specimens.

purpose.value: Determine the austenite lattice parameter a0 of the base alloy.

key_findings.value: For the base alloy no explicit numeric a0 is printed in the text; in the Figure 2 scatter plot the base point (relative alloying = 0) lies just above the 0.358 nm gridline and clearly below 0.359 nm. 2.5 wt.% Al increases a0 by 1.41×10^-3 nm relative to base, whereas 2.5 wt.% Si has little effect - implying little change of the base lattice parameter with Si.

purpose.value: Measure partial dislocation separations d and character angles α to calculate the stacking fault energy (SFE) of the base alloy.

key_findings.value: Base alloy SFE = 26.3 ± 3.0 mJ m^-2 (Figure 3 legend); b0029 states the base alloy SFE is 26.3 mJ m^-2, consistent with 30 mJ m^-2 reported for a similar 15 Ni-11 Cr alloy from TEM analysis of extended dislocation nodes.

source.reason: b0019 gives Eq. (1); b0021 gives the assumed G and ν (74 GPa, 0.3) and the anisotropy test values (66 GPa, 0.43) plus the comment that isotropic values were used; b0018/b0029 describe input of paired (d, α) data into Eq. (1).

simulation_method.value: Analytical calculation of stacking fault energy from measured partial dislocation separation using Eq. (1)

boundary_and_initial_conditions.value: Isotropic elasticity assumed identical for all materials: shear modulus G = 74 GPa and Poisson ratio ν = 0.3. Experimental XRD lattice parameters (a0) were used in Eq. (1). An alternative effect of elastic anisotropy was tested using effective G = 66 GPa and ν = 0.43 determined for a 12 Ni-12 Cr steel.

validation_against_experiment.value: The calculated base alloy SFE (26.3 mJ m^-2) is consistent with the value of 30 mJ m^-2 reported for a similar 15 Ni-11 Cr alloy obtained by TEM analysis of extended dislocation nodes. Applying effective anisotropic elastic constants (G = 66 GPa, ν = 0.43) increased the calculated SFE of the 2.5 Al alloy by ~10% but had little effect on the base and 2.5 Si alloys.

equation_role.value: SFE = G|a0|²(2-ν) / [48π(1-ν)] · (1/d) · [1 - (2ν cos2α)/(2-ν)], where d is partial dislocation separation and α is the perfect dislocation character angle

name.value: G effective (12 Ni-12 Cr steel, anisotropy estimate)
ν effective (12 Ni-12 Cr steel, anisotropy estimate)

value.value: experimental XRD value for the base alloy

model_note.value: Isotropic elastic properties were used in the final SFE calculations because elastic anisotropy was not evaluated in this study and other literature reports an effective ν closer to 0.3 than 0.43. The Williams and Carter correction for partial dislocation strain fields was not applied because not all TEM data were available to assign all necessary parameters.

Stacking fault energy of the base alloy determined by WBDF TEM analysis of dissociated dislocations is 26.3 ± 3.0 mJ m^-2 (Figure 3 legend), and b0029 states the base alloy SFE is 26.3 mJ m^-2, consistent with 30 mJ m^-2 reported for a similar 15 Ni-11 Cr alloy. Source: b0029, b0031, figure_003.

Austenite lattice parameter of the base alloy: the base datum is plotted in Figure 2 at relative alloying = 0 sitting just above the 0.358 nm gridline and clearly below 0.359 nm (small vertical error bar), but no explicit numeric a0 value for the base alloy is printed in the text or figure. Source: figure_002, b0023.

Study-level empirical linear elemental coefficients derived from the three-alloy comparison (Table 2): A^LP(Si) = -0.018×10^-3 nm wt.%-1 [-0.009×10^-3 nm at.%-1], A^LP(Al) = 0.582×10^-3 nm wt.%-1 [0.289]; A^SFE(Si) = -2.6 mJ m^-2 wt.%-1 [-1.3], A^SFE(Al) = 4.9 mJ m^-2 wt.%-1 [2.5]. The Dyson and Holmes reference values are Si ≈0 [≈0] and Al 0.56 [0.28] for A^LP. Source: b0025 / table_002, b0022, b0032.

Estimating A^SFE from the strain-field-corrected data (base and 2.5 Al alloys) gives A^SFE(Al) ≈ 6.9 mJ m^-2 wt.%-1 for this study; literature comparisons: A^SFE(Si) values 1-3.5 mJ m^-2 wt.%-1 (high-Mn literature), thermochemical model A^SFE(Al) ≈ 5.2 mJ m^-2 wt.%-1, Jeong et al. A^SFE(Al) ≈ 6.4 mJ m^-2 wt.%-1, Kim et al. A^SFE(Al) = 11.3 mJ m^-2 wt.%-1. Source: b0033.

The Williams and Carter correction for partial dislocation strain fields (not applied to the reported values) would have little effect (approximately 1 mJ m^-2 or less) on the base and 2.5 Si alloys, but would raise the 2.5 Al alloy SFE to an estimated 44.0 ± 9.8 mJ m^-2. Source: b0029.

Context/limitations stated for extending the study: the base alloy retains austenite at room temperature by Ni and Cr alloying (not by carbon partitioning as in AHSS), and the effects of Si and Al on austenite characteristics are assumed independent of Ni and Cr alloying. Source: b0012.
